decks.title: Metallurgy — Part 1: From ore to metal
goals: Distinguish between a mineral and an ore and name the ores of iron, aluminium and zinc
Choose a concentration method for a given ore and justify it
Distinguish roasting from calcination with an equation for each
Write equations for reducing metal oxides and link the method to the activity series

slides.heading: From rock to metal
slides.body_md: Part 1 — Most metals are found in the earth as compounds mixed with rock. **Metallurgy** is the set of steps that turns such a rock into a pure metal.

visual.alt: Flow of the main steps of metallurgy from ore to metal

slides.narration: Namaste! Very few metals lie in the ground as shiny lumps. Most are locked up as oxides, sulphides or carbonates mixed with sand and rock. Metallurgy is the chain of steps that gets the metal out: first we remove the unwanted rock, then we change the ore into an oxide, and finally we take the oxygen away to leave the metal.

slides.heading: Minerals and ores
slides.body_md: A **mineral** is a naturally occurring compound of a metal in the earth’s crust. An **ore** is a mineral from which the metal can be extracted **conveniently and profitably**. So **every ore is a mineral, but every mineral is not an ore**. The earthy impurities (sand, clay, rock) in an ore are called **gangue** or **matrix**.

rows: Mineral that gives the metal at a profit
Unwanted rock mixed with the ore

visual.alt: Table comparing a mineral, an ore and gangue with aluminium examples

slides.narration: A mineral is any natural compound of a metal found in the earth. An ore is a special mineral: one from which the metal can be extracted easily and at a profit. Clay contains aluminium, but getting the metal out of it costs too much, so clay is only a mineral. Bauxite is both a mineral and an ore. The rock mixed with an ore is called gangue.

slides.heading: Ores of iron, aluminium and zinc
slides.body_md: Learn the name **and** the formula of each ore. Notice the type of compound — it decides how the ore is treated later.

visual.alt: Table of the ores of iron, aluminium and zinc with formulae and type of compound

slides.narration: Iron comes mainly from haematite and magnetite, which are both oxides; magnetite is attracted by a magnet. Aluminium comes from bauxite, a hydrated oxide, and cryolite is a fluoride of aluminium and sodium. Zinc comes from zinc blende, which is a sulphide, and calamine, which is a carbonate. The type of compound tells us which steps the ore will need.

slides.heading: Quick check: ore or mineral?
slides.body_md: Decide what makes a mineral an ore.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about cost and convenience, not just whether the metal is present.

slides.heading: Concentration (dressing) of the ore
slides.body_md:
**Concentration** removes the gangue. The method depends on a **difference in property** between the ore and the gangue.

- **Hydraulic washing** (gravity separation): heavy ore particles stay, light gangue is washed away — e.g. haematite.
- **Magnetic separation**: one part is magnetic — e.g. magnetite.
- **Froth flotation**: sulphide ores — e.g. zinc blende, galena.
- **Chemical method**: bauxite is purified by Baeyer’s process (Part 2).

rows: Ore wetted by oil, gangue by water
Ore dissolves in a reagent, gangue does not

visual.alt: Table of four concentration methods with the property used and an example ore

slides.narration: To remove the gangue we use a property in which the ore and the rock differ. If the ore is much heavier, a stream of water washes the light rock away. If the ore is magnetic, a magnet pulls it out. Sulphide ores are concentrated by froth flotation, and bauxite is purified by a chemical method that dissolves only the alumina.

slides.heading: Froth flotation
slides.body_md: Powdered sulphide ore is mixed with water and a little **pine oil** and air is blown through. Ore particles are **wetted by oil**, cling to air bubbles and rise into the **froth**, which is skimmed off. Gangue particles are **wetted by water** and **sink**.

slides.narration: In froth flotation, the powdered sulphide ore is stirred with water and a little pine oil while air is bubbled through. The oil coats the ore particles, so they stick to the air bubbles and float up in the froth, which is skimmed off. The sandy gangue is wetted by water and sinks to the bottom of the tank.

slides.heading: Roasting and calcination
slides.body_md:
Metals are easiest to extract from **oxides**, so the concentrated ore is first changed into an oxide.

**Roasting:** heating strongly in **excess air**, below the melting point — for **sulphide** ores; sulphur dioxide is given off.

**Calcination:** heating strongly in a **limited supply of air or none** — for **carbonate** and **hydrated** ores; carbon dioxide or water vapour is given off.

visual.alt: Table comparing roasting and calcination by air supply, type of ore, gas given off and an example

slides.narration: Metals are easiest to obtain from their oxides, so the ore is first turned into an oxide. A sulphide ore is roasted: it is heated strongly in plenty of air, and sulphur dioxide is given off. A carbonate or hydrated ore is calcined: it is heated with little or no air, and carbon dioxide or water vapour is driven off.

slides.heading: Worked example: roasting or calcination?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name the process and write the equation for converting (a) galena, PbS, and (b) calamine, ZnCO₃, into oxides.

**(a)** Galena is a **sulphide** → **roasting** in excess air: 2PbS + 3O₂ → 2PbO + 2SO₂.

**(b)** Calamine is a **carbonate** → **calcination**: ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂.

visual.alt: Equation for roasting galena: two lead sulphide plus three oxygen gives two lead oxide plus two sulphur dioxide
visual.caption: Roasting of galena

slides.narration: First look at the type of ore. Galena is lead sulphide, so it is roasted in excess air; oxygen converts it to lead oxide and sulphur dioxide. Calamine is zinc carbonate, so it is calcined; heat alone splits it into zinc oxide and carbon dioxide. The type of ore decides the process every time.

slides.heading: The activity series decides the method of reduction
slides.body_md:
The more reactive a metal, the **more strongly it holds oxygen**, and the harder its oxide is to reduce.

- **K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al:** electrolysis of the **fused** compound (electrolytic reduction).
- **Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu:** reduction of the oxide by **carbon, carbon monoxide or hydrogen**.
- **Hg, Ag:** heating the oxide **alone** (2HgO → 2Hg + O₂).

rows: Reduction by C, CO or H₂

visual.alt: Table linking the position of metals in the activity series to the method of extraction

slides.narration: The activity series tells us how to get each metal. Very reactive metals such as potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium and aluminium hold oxygen so tightly that no chemical can take it away, so we use electrolysis of their molten compounds. Metals in the middle are reduced by carbon, carbon monoxide or hydrogen. Mercury and silver oxides give up oxygen on heating alone.

slides.heading: Reducing the oxide
slides.body_md:
A **reducing agent** removes oxygen from the metal oxide.

- **Hydrogen:** CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O (black → reddish-brown).
- **Carbon (coke):** ZnO + C → Zn + CO; PbO + C → Pb + CO.
- **Carbon monoxide:** Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂; PbO + CO → Pb + CO₂.

Al₂O₃ and MgO are **not** reduced by carbon: aluminium and magnesium have a greater affinity for oxygen than carbon has.

visual.alt: Table of four metal oxides with their reducing agents and balanced equations

slides.narration: A reducing agent pulls oxygen away from the metal. Hydrogen passed over hot black copper oxide leaves reddish brown copper and droplets of water. Coke reduces zinc oxide and lead oxide, and carbon monoxide reduces iron oxide. Aluminium oxide and magnesium oxide are not reduced by carbon, because these metals hold oxygen more strongly than carbon does.

slides.heading: Quick check: method of extraction
slides.body_md: Link a metal to the way it is extracted.
slides.narration: Quick check. The higher a metal is in the activity series, the stronger the method needed.

slides.heading: Worked example: choosing the method
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** How would you obtain (a) lead from lead(II) oxide, (b) sodium from sodium chloride, (c) mercury from mercury(II) oxide? Give a reason each time.

**(a)** Heat with **coke**: PbO + C → Pb + CO — lead is in the middle of the series.

**(b)** **Electrolysis of fused NaCl** — sodium is too reactive for any chemical reducing agent.

**(c)** **Heat alone**: 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂ — mercury is at the bottom of the series.

nodes.label: Where is the metal in the activity series?
Top: electrolysis of the fused compound
Middle: heat oxide with C, CO or H₂

visual.alt: Decision flow for choosing the method of extraction from the position of the metal in the activity series

slides.narration: Always begin with the position of the metal in the activity series. Lead is in the middle, so heating its oxide with coke is enough. Sodium is near the top, so only electrolysis of molten sodium chloride will work. Mercury is near the bottom, so its oxide simply breaks down on heating, giving mercury and oxygen.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Every ore is a mineral; a mineral is an ore only if the metal can be extracted profitably.
Concentration removes gangue: hydraulic washing, magnetic separation, froth flotation or a chemical method.
Roasting (excess air) for sulphides; calcination (little or no air) for carbonates and hydrated ores.
Reactive metals: electrolysis of fused compounds; middle metals: C, CO or H₂; least reactive: heat alone.

visual.alt: Summary table of the steps of metallurgy with their purpose and an example for zinc

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Every ore is a mineral, but only some minerals are ores. The gangue is removed by a method that uses a difference in property. Sulphide ores are roasted and carbonate ores are calcined, giving oxides. The oxide is then reduced by carbon, carbon monoxide or hydrogen, unless the metal is very reactive and needs electrolysis.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Always write the formula with the name of an ore: zinc blende ZnS, calamine ZnCO₃.
Say “excess air” for roasting and “limited air or absence of air” for calcination.
For “give a reason”, link the method to the position of the metal in the activity series.
State the observation too: black CuO turns reddish-brown when reduced by hydrogen.

rows: Calamine is ZnCO₃; zinc blende is ZnS
Calcination in limited air or none

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. Always pair the name of an ore with its formula. Remember that roasting needs plenty of air while calcination needs little or none. When asked for a reason, talk about the position of the metal in the activity series. And in observation questions, mention colour changes, such as black copper oxide turning reddish brown.

slides.heading: Aluminium: from bauxite to metal
slides.body_md: Part 2 — Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the earth’s crust, yet it was once dearer than gold. Two processes made it cheap: **Baeyer’s process** to purify bauxite and the **Hall–Héroult process** to electrolyse alumina.

visual.alt: Flow from impure bauxite through Baeyer’s process to pure alumina and through Hall–Héroult electrolysis to aluminium

slides.narration: Aluminium is the most common metal in the earth’s crust, but it was once more costly than gold, because it was so hard to extract. Two inventions changed that. Baeyer’s process turns impure bauxite into pure alumina, and the Hall–Héroult process passes electricity through molten alumina to give the metal.

slides.heading: Why aluminium needs electrolysis
slides.body_md: Aluminium is **high in the activity series**: it holds oxygen more strongly than carbon, so coke cannot reduce alumina. Alumina must therefore be reduced by **electrolysis**. Because impurities in the ore would also be reduced and spoil the metal, the bauxite is **purified first**.

rows: Not reduced by carbon; electrolysis needed
Solvent (cryolite) needed to work at about 950 °C
Bauxite contains Fe₂O₃ and other impurities
Purified by Baeyer’s process before electrolysis

visual.alt: Table of properties of alumina and their consequences for the extraction of aluminium

slides.narration: Aluminium sits high in the activity series and grips oxygen more strongly than carbon does, so heating alumina with coke does not work. Instead the oxide is decomposed by electricity. Because any impurities would be reduced along with it and spoil the aluminium, the bauxite is first purified, and because alumina melts at a very high temperature, a solvent is used.

slides.heading: Baeyer’s process: step 1, digestion
slides.body_md: Finely ground bauxite is heated with **concentrated sodium hydroxide** solution under pressure (about 150–200 °C). **Alumina dissolves** as soluble **sodium aluminate**; the main impurity, **iron(III) oxide, does not dissolve** and is **filtered off**.

visual.alt: Equation for digestion of bauxite: hydrated alumina plus two sodium hydroxide gives two sodium aluminate plus three water
visual.caption: Digestion of bauxite with sodium hydroxide

slides.narration: In the first step, finely ground bauxite is heated under pressure with concentrated sodium hydroxide solution. Alumina is amphoteric, so it reacts with the alkali and dissolves as sodium aluminate. Iron oxide, the main impurity, is basic and does not dissolve, so it is removed by filtering the hot solution.

slides.heading: Baeyer’s process: steps 2 and 3
slides.body_md:
**Step 2 — precipitation.** The sodium aluminate solution is **diluted** with water and **seeded** with a little freshly made aluminium hydroxide, then stirred. Aluminium hydroxide precipitates.

**Step 3 — ignition.** The aluminium hydroxide is filtered, washed, dried and heated to about **1000 °C**, giving **pure alumina**.

visual.alt: Table of the precipitation and ignition steps of Baeyer’s process with equations

slides.narration: Next, the clear sodium aluminate solution is diluted with water and stirred with a few crystals of fresh aluminium hydroxide. These act as seeds, and white aluminium hydroxide settles out. Finally the precipitate is washed, dried and heated to about one thousand degrees Celsius, which drives out water and leaves pure alumina.

slides.heading: Quick check: Baeyer’s process
slides.body_md: Decide what happens to the impurity in bauxite.
slides.narration: Quick check. Alumina is amphoteric, but iron oxide is basic.

slides.heading: Worked example: alumina from aluminium hydroxide
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** How much alumina is formed when 780 kg of aluminium hydroxide is ignited? (Al = 27, O = 16, H = 1)

**Step 1.** 2Al(OH)₃ → Al₂O₃ + 3H₂O.

**Step 2.** Molar masses: Al(OH)₃ = 27 + 3 × 17 = 78; Al₂O₃ = 2 × 27 + 3 × 16 = 102.

**Step 3.** 156 kg of hydroxide gives 102 kg of alumina, so 780 kg gives 102 × 780 ÷ 156 = **510 kg**.

visual.alt: Table showing that 156 kilograms of aluminium hydroxide gives 102 kilograms of alumina, so 780 kilograms gives 510 kilograms

slides.narration: Write the balanced equation first: two units of aluminium hydroxide give one unit of alumina. The molar mass of the hydroxide is seventy eight and of alumina is one hundred and two. So one hundred and fifty six kilograms of hydroxide gives one hundred and two kilograms of alumina, and five times as much hydroxide gives five hundred and ten kilograms.

slides.heading: The Hall–Héroult cell
slides.body_md:
- **Electrolyte:** pure alumina dissolved in **fused cryolite** (Na₃AlF₆) with a little **fluorspar** (CaF₂), at about **950 °C**.
- **Cathode:** the **carbon lining** of a steel tank.
- **Anodes:** thick **carbon rods** dipping into the electrolyte.
- **Molten aluminium** sinks to the bottom and is tapped off.

visual.alt: The Hall–Héroult cell: carbon anodes dipping into alumina dissolved in fused cryolite, a carbon-lined steel tank as cathode, molten aluminium collecting at the bottom

slides.narration: Here is the cell. A steel tank lined with carbon acts as the cathode. Thick carbon rods dip into the melt from above and act as the anodes. The electrolyte is pure alumina dissolved in molten cryolite with a little fluorspar, at about nine hundred and fifty degrees Celsius. Molten aluminium collects at the bottom and is drawn off.

slides.heading: Cryolite, fluorspar and coke
slides.body_md: **Cryolite** lowers the fusion temperature from about 2050 °C to about 950 °C (saving energy) and **increases the conductivity** of the melt. **Fluorspar** **increases fluidity** (and helps lower the fusion temperature). A layer of **powdered coke** on top **reduces heat loss** and **stops the anodes burning** in air.

rows: Solvent: lowers fusion temperature, raises conductivity
Reduces heat loss; protects anodes from air

visual.alt: Table of cryolite, fluorspar and powdered coke and the purpose of each in the cell

slides.narration: Each addition has a job. Cryolite dissolves the alumina, so the melt works at about nine hundred and fifty degrees instead of over two thousand, and it also conducts electricity better. Fluorspar makes the melt flow more easily. A layer of powdered coke on top keeps the heat in and stops the hot anodes from burning in the air.

slides.heading: Quick check: the electrolytic cell
slides.body_md: Explain a feature of the Hall–Héroult cell.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about what is produced at each electrode and what it can react with.

slides.heading: Electrode reactions
slides.body_md:
In the melt, alumina gives **Al³⁺** and **O²⁻** ions.

- **Cathode (reduction):** Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al
- **Anode (oxidation):** 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻
- **Anodes burn:** C + O₂ → CO₂ and 2C + O₂ → 2CO, so they are **replaced periodically**.

Fresh alumina is added from time to time, so the process runs **continuously**.

visual.alt: Overall equation for the electrolysis of alumina: two alumina give four aluminium and three oxygen
visual.caption: Overall change in the cell

slides.narration: In the melt, alumina provides aluminium ions and oxide ions. At the cathode, each aluminium ion gains three electrons and becomes aluminium metal. At the anode, oxide ions lose electrons and form oxygen. The hot oxygen attacks the carbon anodes, turning them into carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide, so the anodes wear away and must be replaced.

slides.heading: Worked example: aluminium from alumina
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** What mass of aluminium is obtained from 51 tonnes of pure alumina, and what mass of oxygen is released at the anodes? (Al = 27, O = 16)

**Step 1.** Al₂O₃ = 2 × 27 + 3 × 16 = 102; it contains 54 parts aluminium and 48 parts oxygen.

**Step 2.** Aluminium = 54 × 51 ÷ 102 = **27 tonnes**.

**Step 3.** Oxygen = 48 × 51 ÷ 102 = **24 tonnes** — all of it attacks the anodes.

visual.alt: Table splitting 51 tonnes of alumina into 27 tonnes of aluminium and 24 tonnes of oxygen

slides.narration: The molar mass of alumina is one hundred and two, made up of fifty four parts aluminium and forty eight parts oxygen. Fifty one tonnes is exactly half of one hundred and two, so it gives half of fifty four, which is twenty seven tonnes of aluminium, and twenty four tonnes of oxygen. That oxygen is what burns away the carbon anodes.

slides.heading: Alloys and amalgams
slides.body_md: An **alloy** is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals (or a metal and a non-metal). An **amalgam** is an alloy of **mercury** with another metal.

rows: Fe, Cr, Ni, a little C

visual.alt: Table of six alloys with their main constituents and one use of each

slides.narration: An alloy is a uniform mixture of metals, or of a metal with a non-metal such as carbon. Stainless steel is iron with chromium, nickel and a little carbon. Magnalium and duralumin are light aluminium alloys. Brass is copper with zinc, bronze is copper with tin, and solder is lead with tin. When mercury is one of the metals, the alloy is called an amalgam.

slides.heading: Quick check: alloys
slides.body_md: Identify an alloy from its constituents.
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall which aluminium alloy also contains copper and manganese.

slides.heading: Why alloys?

rows: No rust on knives and sinks

visual.alt: Table of four ways alloying improves a metal with an example of each

slides.narration: Why mix metals at all? Pure metals are often too soft, they may corrode, or they may melt at an awkward temperature. Duralumin is much stronger than pure aluminium yet still light. Stainless steel does not rust like iron. Solder melts at a low temperature, which makes it ideal for joining wires, and brass has a pleasing golden colour.

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Baeyer’s process dissolves alumina from bauxite in sodium hydroxide, filters off the iron oxide, and turns the solution back into pure alumina. The Hall–Héroult cell electrolyses that alumina dissolved in molten cryolite, giving aluminium at the cathode and oxygen at the anodes, which burn away. Alloys improve metals for particular uses.

Bronze is copper and tin; brass is copper and zinc — do not swap them.

Remember that the anodes wear away because oxygen burns them, and that aluminium collects at the cathode. And keep bronze and brass apart: bronze has tin, brass has zinc.

notes.title: Metallurgy — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Occurrence of metals: minerals and ores
sections.body_md:
Metals occur **native** (free: gold, platinum) or **combined** as oxides, sulphides, carbonates and other compounds.

- **Mineral:** a naturally occurring compound of a metal in the earth’s crust.
- **Ore:** a mineral from which the metal can be extracted **conveniently and profitably**. Every ore is a mineral; every mineral is not an ore (clay is a mineral of aluminium, not an ore).
- **Gangue (matrix):** the earthy impurities mixed with the ore.

key_terms.definition_md: A mineral from which a metal can be extracted conveniently and profitably.
The unwanted earthy or rocky material mixed with an ore.

rows: Bauxite Al₂O₃·2H₂O; cryolite Na₃AlF₆; corundum Al₂O₃

visual.alt: Table of the ores of iron, aluminium and zinc with formulae

sections.heading: 2. Concentration (dressing) of the ore
sections.body_md:
Concentration removes the gangue, using a property in which ore and gangue differ.

- **Hydraulic washing (gravity separation):** a stream of water washes away the light gangue; heavy ore particles remain (haematite).
- **Magnetic separation:** a magnetic roller separates magnetic ore from non-magnetic gangue (magnetite).
- **Froth flotation:** for **sulphide ores** (zinc blende, galena). Powdered ore + water + **pine oil**; air is blown in. Ore particles are wetted by oil and rise in the froth; gangue is wetted by water and sinks.
- **Chemical method:** bauxite is purified by **Baeyer’s process** (section 5).

key_terms.definition_md: Concentration of a sulphide ore in which oil-wetted ore particles are carried up in a froth while water-wetted gangue sinks.
Concentration that uses a magnet to separate a magnetic ore from non-magnetic gangue, or the reverse.

visual.alt: Table of three ores with their concentration method and the reason

sections.heading: 3. Roasting and calcination
sections.body_md:
The concentrated ore is changed into an **oxide**, which is easier to reduce.

| Roasting | Calcination |
|---|---|
| Strong heating in **excess air**, below the melting point | Strong heating in **limited air or none** |
| For **sulphide** ores | For **carbonate** and **hydrated** ores |
| Gives SO₂ | Gives CO₂ or H₂O |

Both also remove volatile impurities and leave the ore porous.

key_terms.definition_md: Heating a sulphide ore strongly in excess air, below its melting point, to convert it into the oxide.
Heating a carbonate or hydrated ore strongly in a limited supply of air or in its absence to convert it into the oxide.

visual.alt: Table of three ores with the process used and the gas given off

sections.heading: 4. Reduction and the activity series
sections.body_md:
The method of reduction depends on the position of the metal in the **activity series**.

- **K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al** (most reactive): **electrolysis of fused compounds**. Their oxides are too stable for carbon, and in aqueous solution hydrogen would be discharged instead.
- **Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu**: oxide reduced by **carbon (coke), carbon monoxide or hydrogen** on heating.
- **Hg, Ag** (least reactive): heating the oxide alone, e.g. 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂.

Al₂O₃ and MgO are not reduced by carbon because aluminium and magnesium have a greater affinity for oxygen than carbon has.

key_terms.definition_md: A substance that removes oxygen from (or adds electrons to) another substance, itself being oxidised.
Extraction of a reactive metal by electrolysing its fused compound; the metal ions gain electrons at the cathode.

rows: Reduction by C, CO or H₂

sections.heading: 5. Purification of bauxite: Baeyer’s process
sections.body_md:
Bauxite contains iron(III) oxide (and other impurities) that would spoil the aluminium, so it is purified first.

1. **Digestion:** finely ground bauxite is heated with **concentrated NaOH** under pressure (about 150–200 °C). Alumina dissolves as sodium aluminate; **Fe₂O₃ does not dissolve** and is filtered off.
2. **Precipitation:** the solution is **diluted** and **seeded** with fresh Al(OH)₃ and stirred; Al(OH)₃ precipitates.
3. **Ignition:** Al(OH)₃ is washed, dried and heated to about **1000 °C** to give **pure alumina**.

key_terms.definition_md: Purification of bauxite by dissolving alumina in hot concentrated sodium hydroxide, filtering off impurities, precipitating aluminium hydroxide and igniting it to alumina.
Adding a few crystals of a substance to a solution to start its precipitation.

visual.alt: Table of the stages of Baeyer’s process and the form of aluminium at each

sections.heading: 6. Extraction of aluminium: Hall–Héroult process
sections.body_md:
- **Electrolyte:** pure alumina dissolved in fused **cryolite** (Na₃AlF₆) with a little **fluorspar** (CaF₂); about **950 °C**.
- **Cathode:** carbon lining of the steel tank. **Anodes:** thick carbon rods dipping into the electrolyte.
- **Cryolite:** lowers the fusion temperature (from about 2050 °C) and increases conductivity. **Fluorspar:** increases fluidity. **Powdered coke** on top: reduces heat loss and protects the anodes from air.
- Molten aluminium collects at the bottom and is tapped off; fresh alumina is added, so the process is continuous.
- Oxygen formed at the anodes burns them (C + O₂ → CO₂; 2C + O₂ → 2CO), so the **anodes are replaced periodically**.

Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al. Anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻.

key_terms.definition_md: Na₃AlF₆; the solvent for alumina in the Hall–Héroult cell, which lowers the fusion temperature and raises conductivity.
CaF₂; added to the electrolyte to increase its fluidity.

visual.alt: Table of the parts of the Hall–Héroult cell

sections.heading: 7. Alloys and amalgams
sections.body_md:
An **alloy** is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal and a non-metal. An **amalgam** is an alloy containing **mercury**.

Alloys are preferred because they can be **harder and stronger**, **resist corrosion**, have a **lower melting point**, or look better than the pure metal.

key_terms.definition_md: A homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal and a non-metal.
An alloy in which one of the metals is mercury.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing calamine as ZnS (it is ZnCO₃; zinc blende is ZnS).
- Saying calcination is done in excess air.
- Saying aluminium forms at the anode, or that cryolite is an electrode.
- Forgetting that the anodes are burnt away by oxygen.
- Swapping brass (Cu, Zn) and bronze (Cu, Sn).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Equations (1 mark): correct formulae and balancing; add the condition (heat, excess air) where asked.
- Reasons (1 mark each): link to the activity series, affinity for oxygen or a property difference.
- Hall–Héroult questions: electrolyte, electrodes, electrode reactions and the roles of cryolite, fluorspar and coke.

questions.stem_md: Haematite (Fe₂O₃) and iron pyrites (FeS₂) both contain iron, but only haematite is treated as an ore of iron. The reason is that from haematite iron can be:

options.text_md: separated by dissolving the rock in water
extracted conveniently and at a profit

questions.solution_md: An ore is a mineral from which the metal can be extracted conveniently and profitably; pyrites is mainly used for its sulphur — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Calamine is an ore of zinc. Its chemical formula is:
questions.solution_md: Calamine is zinc carbonate; ZnS is zinc blende — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Every mineral of a metal is also an ore of that metal.
questions.solution_md: False: every ore is a mineral, but a mineral is an ore only if the metal can be extracted from it conveniently and profitably (clay is a mineral of aluminium, not an ore).

questions.stem_md: Name the sulphide ore of zinc and write its formula.

answer.model_answer_md: Zinc blende, ZnS.

questions.solution_md: Zinc blende.

questions.stem_md: Name the ore of iron whose particles are attracted by a magnet, and write its formula.

answer.model_answer_md: Magnetite, Fe₃O₄.

questions.solution_md: Magnetite.

questions.stem_md: A mining company tests two rocks. Rock P is 60% haematite, Fe₂O₃, by mass. Rock Q contains only 3% iron, locked in a silicate that no cheap process can break down. (a) Which rock would the company work as an ore of iron? Give a reason. (b) Calculate the mass of iron present in 1000 kg of that rock. (Fe = 56, O = 16)

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Rock P, because iron can be extracted from haematite conveniently and at a profit, which is what makes a mineral an ore; in Q the iron is locked in a silicate and cannot be extracted profitably. (b) Fe₂O₃ is 70% iron (112 ÷ 160). Mass of Fe₂O₃ in 1000 kg of P = 600 kg, so mass of iron = 0.70 × 600 = 420 kg.

questions.solution_md: Ore: profitable extraction (P). Iron = 70% of 600 kg = 420 kg.

marking_scheme.step: (a) P chosen, with the profit reason

questions.stem_md: Calculate the percentage by mass of iron in pure haematite, Fe₂O₃. (Fe = 56, O = 16)
questions.solution_md: Molar mass of $\ce{Fe2O3} = 2 \times 56 + 3 \times 16 = 160$. Mass of iron in it $= 2 \times 56 = 112$. Percentage of iron $= \dfrac{112}{160} \times 100 = 70$, so 70%.

questions.stem_md: A powdered iron ore is attracted by a magnet, but the rocky gangue mixed with it is not. The best method to concentrate this ore is:
questions.solution_md: One component is magnetic and the other is not — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a froth flotation tank holding finely powdered zinc blende mixed with sand and water, air is blown in but an operator forgets to add the pine oil. The most likely result is that:

options.text_md: the sand rises into the froth, because it is wetted by air
little ore reaches the froth, because the water-wetted sulphide particles do not cling to the air bubbles, so ore and sand stay together
the zinc blende is converted into zinc oxide by the air
the froth carries even more ore, because air alone wets sulphides

questions.solution_md: Without oil the sulphide particles are wetted by water like the gangue, so the air bubbles do not lift them and no separation occurs. Sand is wetted by water in any case and stays in the tank. Zinc blende is not oxidised at room temperature in the tank, so roasting does not occur — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Four crushed ore–gangue mixtures (approximate densities in g/cm³) are each run over a sloping, shaking table with a stream of water. In which mixture does hydraulic washing give the best concentration of the ore?

options.text_md: an ore (3.0) mixed with a gangue (3.1)

questions.solution_md: Washing carries away the lighter material and leaves the heavier one behind. Only haematite and sand differ greatly, with the ore the heavier. Barytes is denser than zinc blende, so the ore would be washed away; the last two pairs differ by too little to separate — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Froth flotation is a suitable method for concentrating zinc blende.

**Reason (R):** Sulphide ore particles are wetted by oil, while the gangue particles are wetted by water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R is the principle on which the method works — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Match each ore in Column A with the most suitable method of concentration in Column B.
questions.solution_md: Magnetite → magnetic separation (magnetic ore); zinc blende → froth flotation (sulphide); heavy haematite → hydraulic washing; bauxite → chemical method (Baeyer’s process).

questions.stem_md: Suggest, with a reason in each case, how you would concentrate: (a) magnetite mixed with non-magnetic rock; (b) zinc blende; (c) haematite mixed with light sandy gangue.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Magnetic separation: magnetite is attracted by the magnet and the rock is not. (b) Froth flotation: the sulphide particles are wetted by pine oil and rise with the froth while the gangue sinks. (c) Hydraulic washing (gravity separation): the heavy haematite particles stay behind while the light sand is washed away.

questions.solution_md: Magnetic; froth flotation; gravity.

questions.stem_md: A sample of 97 g of pure zinc blende, ZnS, is roasted completely in excess air. What volume of sulphur dioxide, measured at STP, is given off? (Zn = 65, S = 32; one mole of a gas occupies 22.4 L at STP)
questions.solution_md: Molar mass of ZnS = 97, so 97 g is 1 mol. 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂: 2 mol ZnS give 2 mol SO₂, so 1 mol gives 1 mol, which is 22.4 L at STP — option (a). (33.6 L uses the 3 of 3O₂; 44.8 L takes 2 mol of gas; 11.2 L halves it.)

questions.stem_md: A dull white ore is heated strongly in a covered crucible with very little air. An odourless gas is given off that turns lime water milky, there is no choking smell, and the residue is a solid that is yellow when hot and white on cooling. The change is best described as:

options.text_md: roasting of a sulphide ore, leaving zinc oxide
reduction of zinc oxide by carbon, leaving zinc metal
calcination of a carbonate ore, leaving zinc oxide
concentration of the ore, leaving pure calamine

questions.solution_md: An odourless gas that clouds lime water is CO₂, not the choking SO₂ of roasting; so the ore is a carbonate heated in limited air (calcination), and the residue that is yellow when hot and white when cold is ZnO: ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Roasting is carried out in excess air and is used mainly for sulphide ores.
questions.solution_md: True: the sulphide is oxidised to the metal oxide and sulphur dioxide.

questions.stem_md: Write a balanced equation for the roasting of galena, PbS.

answer.model_answer_md: 2PbS + 3O₂ → 2PbO + 2SO₂ (heated in excess air).

questions.solution_md: Equation.

questions.stem_md: Write a balanced equation for the calcination of calamine.

answer.model_answer_md: ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂ (on heating).

questions.solution_md: Equation.

questions.stem_md: Two concentrated ores are heated. Ore E, heated in excess air, gives a pungent gas that turns acidified potassium dichromate paper from orange to green. Ore F, heated in a limited supply of air, gives an odourless gas that turns lime water milky. (a) Name the process applied to E and to F, and the type of ore (sulphide, carbonate) each most probably is. (b) Name the gas from each and give the formula of one zinc ore that could be E and one that could be F.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) E: roasting, so E is a sulphide ore; F: calcination, so F is a carbonate ore. (b) E gives sulphur dioxide (the gas that turns dichromate green); a zinc ore that fits is zinc blende, ZnS. F gives carbon dioxide (it turns lime water milky); a zinc ore that fits is calamine, ZnCO₃.

questions.solution_md: Pungent gas, dichromate green: SO₂, so a sulphide roasted in excess air; odourless gas, lime water milky: CO₂, so a carbonate calcined.

marking_scheme.step: (a) processes and ore types from the observations

questions.stem_md: Which of these metals is obtained by electrolysis of its fused chloride and not by heating its oxide with coke?
questions.solution_md: Magnesium is high in the activity series; its oxide is too stable for carbon to reduce — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Dry hydrogen is passed over heated black copper(II) oxide in a hard-glass tube. The observation is:

options.text_md: the black solid turns white and a brown gas is given off
the black solid turns blue and dissolves
the black solid turns reddish-brown and droplets of a colourless liquid collect in the cooler part of the tube
there is no change, because hydrogen cannot reduce metal oxides

questions.solution_md: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O: copper is reddish-brown and water condenses — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student heats 16.0 g of an oxide of iron in a stream of carbon monoxide until the mass stops changing. Only 11.2 g of iron remains. Using Fe = 56 and O = 16, the oxide must be:
questions.solution_md: Oxygen removed = 16.0 − 11.2 = 4.8 g. Moles: Fe = 11.2 ÷ 56 = 0.2; O = 4.8 ÷ 16 = 0.3. The ratio Fe : O = 2 : 3, so the oxide is Fe₂O₃ — option (b). (0.2 mol of iron in FeO would come from only 14.4 g of oxide, and in Fe₃O₄ from about 15.5 g; Fe₃O₂ comes from reversing the subscripts of 2 : 3.)

questions.stem_md: Metal X is obtained by electrolysis of its fused chloride, metal Y by heating its oxide with coke, and metal Z by heating its oxide alone. The order of decreasing reactivity is:
questions.solution_md: The more reactive the metal, the harder its compounds are to reduce: electrolysis (most reactive), then carbon, then heat alone (least reactive) — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sodium is extracted by electrolysis of fused sodium chloride.

**Reason (R):** Sodium chloride is a covalent compound that does not conduct electricity when molten.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false: sodium chloride is ionic and conducts when molten — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Mercury(II) oxide gives mercury when it is heated alone, without any reducing agent.
questions.solution_md: True: 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂ on heating; mercury is low in the activity series.

questions.stem_md: Write a balanced equation, with the condition, for the reduction of copper(II) oxide by hydrogen.

answer.model_answer_md: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O (on heating).

questions.solution_md: Equation with heat.

questions.stem_md: Write a balanced equation for the reduction of lead(II) oxide by carbon.

answer.model_answer_md: PbO + C → Pb + CO (on heating).

questions.solution_md: Equation.

questions.stem_md: Name the method used to extract potassium from its compounds.

answer.model_answer_md: Electrolysis of fused (molten) potassium chloride or potassium hydroxide.

questions.solution_md: Electrolytic reduction.

questions.stem_md: Magnesium is extracted by electrolysis of fused magnesium chloride, while lead is obtained by heating lead(II) oxide with coke. Explain this difference.

answer.model_answer_md: Magnesium is high in the activity series and has a greater affinity for oxygen than carbon, so carbon cannot remove oxygen from magnesium oxide; the strong reducing action of electrolysis (gain of electrons at the cathode) is needed. Lead is much lower in the series, so carbon readily removes oxygen from lead(II) oxide: PbO + C → Pb + CO.

questions.solution_md: Position in the series; affinity for oxygen.

marking_scheme.step: Magnesium: reactive, oxide not reduced by carbon
Lead: less reactive, reduced by carbon

questions.stem_md: A sample of concentrated calamine is to be turned into zinc. (a) Name the process that changes calamine into zinc oxide and write its equation. (b) Write the equation for the reduction of zinc oxide by coke. (c) Why can zinc oxide be reduced by coke while magnesium oxide cannot?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Calcination: ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂. (b) ZnO + C → Zn + CO (on strong heating). (c) On strong heating, carbon has a greater affinity for oxygen than zinc has, so it removes oxygen from zinc oxide; magnesium has a greater affinity for oxygen than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce magnesium oxide.

questions.solution_md: Calcination; reduction; affinity for oxygen.

questions.stem_md: Three metal oxides P, Q and R are tested. P gives its metal and oxygen when heated alone. Q gives its metal only when heated strongly with coke. R is not reduced by coke even at very high temperatures. (a) Suggest one oxide that fits each of P, Q and R. (b) Arrange the three metals in increasing order of reactivity. (c) Name the method by which the metal of R is obtained.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) P: mercury(II) oxide; Q: zinc oxide (or lead(II) oxide); R: aluminium oxide (or magnesium oxide). (b) P < Q < R (mercury < zinc < aluminium). (c) Electrolysis of a fused compound of the metal (electrolytic reduction).

questions.solution_md: Identify from reducibility; reactivity order; electrolysis.

questions.stem_md: In Baeyer's process, finely ground bauxite is heated with concentrated sodium hydroxide solution under pressure. The iron(III) oxide present as an impurity:

options.text_md: does not dissolve and is removed by filtration
is reduced to iron and sinks
escapes from the solution as a gas

questions.solution_md: Only the amphoteric alumina dissolves (as sodium aluminate); basic iron(III) oxide stays undissolved — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Two equal portions of the filtered sodium aluminate solution from Baeyer's process are kept apart. Portion 1 is left concentrated and unseeded. Portion 2 is diluted with water and stirred with a little freshly made aluminium hydroxide. After some hours, the observation most likely is that:

options.text_md: portion 1 has deposited more, because it holds more sodium aluminate
neither portion has deposited anything, because aluminium hydroxide stays dissolved in water
portion 2 has deposited much more solid aluminium hydroxide than portion 1
portion 2 has deposited iron(III) oxide instead of aluminium hydroxide

questions.solution_md: Dilution favours the hydrolysis NaAlO₂ + 2H₂O → NaOH + Al(OH)₃, and the added solid gives crystals on which more aluminium hydroxide can grow, so portion 2 yields far more precipitate. Iron(III) oxide was removed earlier by filtration — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the action of sodium hydroxide solution on bauxite, Al₂O₃·2H₂O, in Baeyer's process.

answer.model_answer_md: Al₂O₃·2H₂O + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + 3H₂O.

questions.solution_md: Equation.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the action of strong heat (about 1000 °C) on aluminium hydroxide.

answer.model_answer_md: 2Al(OH)₃ → Al₂O₃ + 3H₂O.

questions.solution_md: Equation.

questions.stem_md: In Baeyer's process, aluminium hydroxide is heated strongly to give pure ___, which is then sent for electrolysis.
questions.solution_md: Pure **alumina** (aluminium oxide).

questions.stem_md: In Baeyer's process, 820 g of pure sodium aluminate, NaAlO₂, is changed completely into aluminium hydroxide by dilution with water. Write the balanced equation and calculate the mass of aluminium hydroxide formed. (Na = 23, Al = 27, O = 16, H = 1)

answer.model_answer_md: NaAlO₂ + 2H₂O → NaOH + Al(OH)₃↓. Molar mass of NaAlO₂ = 23 + 27 + 32 = 82, so 820 g is 10 mol. One mole gives one mole of Al(OH)₃ (molar mass 27 + 51 = 78), so 10 mol gives 780 g of aluminium hydroxide.

questions.solution_md: Hydrolysis equation; 10 mol NaAlO₂ give 10 mol Al(OH)₃ = 780 g.

questions.stem_md: A trial cell is filled with fused pure alumina alone, with no cryolite or fluorspar, between the carbon electrodes. Compared with the normal Hall–Héroult cell, the trial cell:

options.text_md: would need a temperature above 2000 °C and would conduct poorly, so it would be very costly to run
would work at about 950 °C but give impure aluminium
would deposit aluminium at the anode instead of the cathode
would give hydrogen at the cathode instead of aluminium

questions.solution_md: Alumina melts at about 2050 °C, and the fused oxide conducts poorly; cryolite is what lets the cell run near 950 °C with good conductivity. Without it the cell must be kept far hotter for little current. The electrode reactions (aluminium at the cathode) are unchanged, and there is no water, so no hydrogen — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the Hall–Héroult cell, the carbon anodes have to be replaced from time to time because:

options.text_md: oxygen set free at the anodes burns them away as oxides of carbon
they melt at the temperature of the cell

questions.solution_md: C + O₂ → CO₂ and 2C + O₂ → 2CO — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student tries to make aluminium by passing a current through a solution of aluminium sulphate in water, using inert electrodes. At the cathode:

options.text_md: aluminium is deposited, as in the Hall–Héroult cell
oxygen gas is given off, because oxide ions from the sulphate are reduced
a layer of alumina forms on the cathode
hydrogen gas is given off and no aluminium is formed, because hydrogen ions from water are discharged in preference to Al³⁺

questions.solution_md: Aluminium is high in the activity series, so in aqueous solution H⁺ ions from water are discharged before Al³⁺ (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂). Aluminium is therefore obtained only from a fused, water-free electrolyte. Oxygen is a product at the anode, not the cathode — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Cryolite is added to alumina in the Hall–Héroult cell.

**Reason (R):** Cryolite is a mineral of aluminium.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but cryolite is added to lower the fusion temperature and raise the conductivity, not because it contains aluminium — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A layer of powdered coke is spread over the surface of the electrolyte in the Hall–Héroult cell.

**Reason (R):** The coke layer reduces heat loss from the surface and stops the anodes burning in air at the surface.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The formula of cryolite, used as a solvent for alumina, is ___.
questions.solution_md: **Na₃AlF₆** (Na3AlF6), sodium aluminium fluoride.

questions.stem_md: State the purpose of adding fluorspar to the electrolyte in the Hall–Héroult cell.

answer.model_answer_md: Fluorspar (CaF₂) increases the fluidity of the electrolyte (and helps lower its fusion temperature).

questions.solution_md: Fluidity.

questions.stem_md: Write the equation for the reaction at the anode during the electrolysis of fused alumina.

answer.model_answer_md: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ (or 6O²⁻ → 3O₂ + 12e⁻).

questions.solution_md: Oxide ions lose electrons.

questions.stem_md: Explain, with an equation, why the anodes of the Hall–Héroult cell must be replaced periodically while the cathode lasts much longer.

answer.model_answer_md: Oxygen is liberated at the hot carbon anodes and burns them: C + O₂ → CO₂ (and 2C + O₂ → 2CO), so they wear away. At the cathode aluminium is deposited; nothing there reacts with the carbon lining.

questions.solution_md: Anode oxidised by oxygen; cathode receives aluminium.

marking_scheme.step: Anode burnt by oxygen, with equation

questions.stem_md: What mass of aluminium, in kg, can be obtained from 204 kg of pure alumina, Al₂O₃? (Al = 27, O = 16)
questions.solution_md: Molar mass of $\ce{Al2O3} = 2 \times 27 + 3 \times 16 = 102$, and it contains $2 \times 27 = 54$ parts of aluminium. Mass of aluminium $= \dfrac{54}{102} \times 204 = 108$, so 108 kg.

questions.stem_md: During the electrolysis of fused alumina, 54 g of aluminium is deposited at the cathode. What volume of oxygen, measured at STP, is set free at the anodes, in litres? (Al = 27; one mole of a gas occupies 22.4 L at STP)
questions.solution_md: Overall: $\ce{2Al2O3 -> 4Al + 3O2}$. Moles of aluminium $= \dfrac{54}{27} = 2$. Moles of oxygen $= 2 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 1.5$. Volume $= 1.5 \times 22.4 = 33.6$, so 33.6 L.

questions.stem_md: A plant manager reads these figures. Alumina melts at about 2050 °C and is a poor conductor when fused; cryolite melts at about 1010 °C and is a good conductor when fused; a mixture of cryolite with a little alumina melts at about 950 °C. (a) Use the figures to give two reasons why alumina is dissolved in fused cryolite instead of being electrolysed alone. (b) The cell is allowed to cool to 800 °C with current still switched on. Predict what happens and why. (c) Cryolite alone melts easily and conducts well, so why is the cell not simply filled with fused cryolite?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Dissolving alumina in cryolite brings the working temperature down from 2050 °C to about 950 °C, and the cryolite melt is a good conductor whereas fused alumina is not. (b) 800 °C is below the melting point of the mixture (about 950 °C), so the electrolyte begins to solidify into a crust; the ions cannot move, the current falls and the cell stops working. (c) The aim is to obtain aluminium from alumina; cryolite is only the solvent and conductor, and alumina must keep being supplied as the source of aluminium.

questions.solution_md: Lower temperature and better conduction; solidification below 950 °C; alumina is the source of aluminium.

marking_scheme.step: (c) alumina is the source of aluminium

questions.stem_md: Which alloy contains aluminium together with small amounts of copper, magnesium and manganese?
questions.solution_md: Duralumin: about 95% Al, 4% Cu, 0.5% Mg, 0.5% Mn — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Stainless steel is chosen for surgical instruments and kitchen sinks mainly because the chromium and nickel in it:

options.text_md: make it resist rusting and corrosion
lower its melting point below that of tin
make it a poor conductor of heat

questions.solution_md: Stainless steel does not rust and keeps a bright surface — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An engineer needs a light but strong alloy for the beam of a chemical balance. The most suitable choice is:

options.text_md: stainless steel (iron, chromium, nickel and carbon)

questions.solution_md: Magnalium is light (both metals have low density) and stronger than aluminium — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Bronze is an alloy of copper and zinc.

**Reason (R):** Alloys are usually harder than the pure metals from which they are made.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A is false: bronze is copper and tin (brass is copper and zinc). R is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Lead melts at about 327 °C and tin at about 232 °C. A technician must join electronic parts that must not be heated above 200 °C. She reasons that an alloy of lead and tin could be used even though neither metal alone melts low enough.
questions.solution_md: True: an alloy usually melts at a lower temperature than its constituents, and lead–tin solder melts at about 183 °C, below both metals and below 200 °C.

questions.stem_md: An alloy in which one of the metals is mercury is called an ___.
questions.solution_md: An **amalgam** (for example, sodium amalgam or the silver–tin amalgam used in tooth fillings).

questions.stem_md: State the two main metals in bronze and one use of bronze.

answer.model_answer_md: Copper and tin; used for statues, medals or bells.

questions.solution_md: Cu and Sn; one use.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why an alloy is often used instead of a pure metal, with one example for each reason.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) An alloy is harder and stronger: duralumin is much stronger than pure aluminium and is used for aircraft bodies. (2) An alloy resists corrosion better: stainless steel does not rust, unlike pure iron. (Also accepted: lower melting point, as in solder.)

questions.solution_md: Two reasons with examples.

questions.stem_md:
Complete each sentence by choosing the correct word from the bracket.

(a) Removing the gangue from a crushed ore is called ___ (concentration / calcination).

(b) Zinc blende is concentrated by ___ (froth flotation / magnetic separation).

(c) Heating a carbonate ore in a limited supply of air is called ___ (roasting / calcination).
questions.solution_md: (a) **concentration**; (b) **froth flotation**; (c) **calcination**.

questions.stem_md: Match each alloy in Column A with its main constituent metals in Column B.

match_right.text_md: Iron, chromium, nickel and a little carbon

questions.solution_md: Stainless steel → iron, chromium, nickel, carbon; magnalium → aluminium, magnesium; duralumin → aluminium, copper, magnesium, manganese; bronze → copper, tin; solder → lead, tin.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define (i) a mineral and (ii) an ore. [2]

(b) Name one ore each of iron and zinc and write their formulae. [2]

(c) Potassium, zinc and mercury are extracted by different methods. Name the method used for each, and give a reason for the method used for potassium. [3]

(d) Write balanced equations for: (i) the reduction of zinc oxide by carbon; (ii) the reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon monoxide; (iii) the reduction of copper(II) oxide by hydrogen. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) A mineral is a naturally occurring compound of a metal found in the earth’s crust. (ii) An ore is a mineral from which the metal can be extracted conveniently and profitably.

(b) Iron: haematite, Fe₂O₃ (or magnetite, Fe₃O₄). Zinc: zinc blende, ZnS (or calamine, ZnCO₃).

(c) Potassium: electrolysis of its fused chloride; zinc: reduction of its oxide by carbon (coke); mercury: heating its oxide alone. Potassium is very reactive and its compounds are very stable; no chemical reducing agent such as carbon can reduce them.

(d) (i) ZnO + C → Zn + CO. (ii) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. (iii) CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; ores; methods and reason; equations.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by the concentration of an ore? Name two physical methods of concentration. [2]

(b) Explain the principle of froth flotation and the role of pine oil. [2]

(c) State one difference between roasting and calcination, and write one balanced equation for each. [3]

(d) A sulphide ore is converted into its oxide before reduction. (i) Why is this done? (ii) Name the gas given off. (iii) Suggest one way of preventing this gas from polluting the air. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Removing the unwanted earthy matter (gangue) from the crushed ore. Physical methods: hydraulic washing and magnetic separation (or froth flotation).

(b) Sulphide ore particles are wetted by oil and gangue particles by water. Pine oil coats the ore particles, which stick to air bubbles and rise in the froth, while the gangue sinks.

(c) Roasting is done in excess air (for sulphide ores); calcination in a limited supply of air or none (for carbonate and hydrated ores). Roasting: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂. Calcination: ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂.

(d) (i) An oxide is reduced by carbon much more easily than a sulphide. (ii) Sulphur dioxide. (iii) Collect it and use it to make sulphuric acid (the Contact process).

questions.solution_md: Concentration; flotation principle; roasting and calcination; reason, gas, prevention.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the formula of bauxite and name the main impurity removed from it in Baeyer's process. [2]

(b) Write the balanced equation for the digestion of bauxite with sodium hydroxide, and state what happens to the impurity. [2]

(c) Write balanced equations for (i) the formation of aluminium hydroxide from sodium aluminate and (ii) the action of heat on aluminium hydroxide, and state why seeding is used in step (i). [3]

(d) A batch of 312 g of pure aluminium hydroxide is heated strongly. Calculate the mass of alumina formed, and explain why the alumina must be pure before electrolysis. (Al = 27, O = 16, H = 1) [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\ce{Al2O3.2H2O}$; the main impurity is iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃.

(b) $\ce{Al2O3.2H2O + 2NaOH -> 2NaAlO2 + 3H2O}$. Iron(III) oxide does not dissolve and is filtered off.

(c) (i) $\ce{NaAlO2 + 2H2O -> NaOH + Al(OH)3}$. (ii) $\ce{2Al(OH)3 -> Al2O3 + 3H2O}$ at about 1000 °C. Seeding with fresh aluminium hydroxide starts the precipitation.

(d) Molar mass of $\ce{Al(OH)3} = 27 + 3 \times 17 = 78$; of $\ce{Al2O3} = 2 \times 27 + 3 \times 16 = 102$. Two moles (156 g) of the hydroxide give 102 g of alumina, so the mass of alumina $= \dfrac{102}{156} \times 312 = 204$, that is 204 g. Impurities would be reduced too and would contaminate the aluminium.

questions.solution_md: Formula and impurity; digestion; precipitation and ignition; mass of alumina from the 2 : 1 mole ratio.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the composition of the electrolyte used in the Hall–Héroult process and the temperature at which the cell works. [2]

(b) Name the cathode and the anode of the cell. [2]

(c) Write the equations for the reactions at the cathode and the anode, and the overall equation for the electrolysis of alumina. [3]

(d) Give one reason each for: (i) adding cryolite; (ii) replacing the anodes from time to time; (iii) spreading powdered coke over the electrolyte. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Pure alumina dissolved in fused cryolite (Na₃AlF₆), with a little fluorspar (CaF₂); about 950 °C.

(b) Cathode: the carbon lining of the steel tank. Anode: thick carbon (graphite) rods dipping into the electrolyte.

(c) Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al. Anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻. Overall: 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂.

(d) (i) It lowers the fusion temperature of the electrolyte and increases its conductivity. (ii) Oxygen liberated at the anodes burns the carbon to CO and CO₂. (iii) It reduces heat loss and prevents the anodes burning in air.

questions.solution_md: Electrolyte; electrodes; equations; reasons.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define (i) an alloy and (ii) an amalgam. [2]

(b) Give two ways in which the properties of an alloy differ from those of its main metal. [2]

(c) State the constituent metals of (i) duralumin, (ii) magnalium and (iii) solder. [3]

(d) Choose the most suitable alloy from brass, bronze, duralumin and stainless steel for each use, and give a reason: (i) the body of an aircraft; (ii) a set of surgical knives; (iii) a statue to stand outdoors. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal and a non-metal. (ii) An amalgam is an alloy in which one of the metals is mercury.

(b) An alloy is usually harder and stronger, has a lower melting point, and resists corrosion better (any two).

(c) (i) Aluminium, copper, magnesium and manganese. (ii) Aluminium and magnesium. (iii) Lead and tin.

(d) (i) Duralumin: light and strong. (ii) Stainless steel: does not rust and stays sharp and clean. (iii) Bronze: hard and resists corrosion in air and rain.
